newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM says officials Khmer Rouge hostages.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM says officials Khmer Rouge hostages.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen on Thursday said Khmer Rouge hardliners are holding 15 government officials as hostages.

"I am worried about the safety of our brothers, but we are trying to find a solution," he told reporters. He was referring to pilots and officials, including Deputy Governor of Siem Reap province Hem Bunheng, missing in northern Cambodia.

The group flew by helicopter into an area near the hardliner base of Anlong Veng on the Thai border on February 14 in hopes of recruiting defectors, including feared one-legged commander Ta Mok. But they never returned from their mission.
"They are not being kept for negotiation, but they are being kept as hostages. But we hope our brothers (the Khmer Rouge) in Anlong Veng won't do anything to them," Hun Sen said.

Hun Sen, speaking to reporters after a signing ceremony between his Cambodian People's Party and a smaller party, said he could not give details on negotiations for fear of jeopardising efforts to release the 15.

But he hinted force might be an option if the problem was not resolved, while stressing: "Anlong Veng cannot be a state within a state and Anlong Veng must accept the authority of the kingdom of Cambodia."
The government has sent officials to the Thai border to meet with hardline rebels each day since the incident.
But while the trips yielded about 150 Khmer Rouge defectors on Monday, no others have followed suit and they have been unable to secure the release of the 15 men.
Government officials fear the missing team is being used to win leverage in negotiations for further defections.

The Khmer Rouge, which led the brutal 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime, signed a U.N.-sponsored peace pact in 1991 but later reneged on the deal and have been fighting the coalition government elected in 1993.
In recent months, they have been crippled by defections, leaving fewer than 2,000 fighters concentrated in Anlong Veng.
Despite their military decline, the rebels have gained political muscle by exploiting rifts in the coalition government.
Co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen have been competing to win ex-guerrillas over to their respective parties, FUNCINPEC and the Cambodian People's Party.
